subject: utilize a database+compute(), or a directory of .rds files

messages.author: d4c7167e7e0c951f
messages.subject: utilize a database+compute(), or a directory of .rds files
parts:
Hello, I've been reading database vignette and got excited by the compute() command for use of Shiny reactive filtering on a large database. 

But this got me thinking.  For a large database, say 1-2 TB, and shiny app on a very large machine, do you think it is better practice to: 

A.  As user filters, use compute(), and reactively update results with the resulting remote tbl.

B.  Don't use a database.  Break the database into a directory of .rds files based on the first filter levels.  Each .rds fits into memory easily, so for the first filter, readRDS( the appropriate .rds), and reactively filter the .rds from there as user applies additional filters.  Same as before - reactively update results with the local tbl.

Breaking into .rds files could be extended further to keep each file small enough for memory.  It seems like the advice would be to use strategy B until the data can't fit onto disk. 

Seems strange to me not to use a database with this much data, so I wanted to know what the recommended or best practice is.  Thanks.

messages.subject: Re: utilize a database+compute(), or a directory of .rds files
parts:
I can't imagine why you'd want to do B - it seems like a lot more work.
Hadley

parts:
Thank you for the response.  Both ways are straightforward - in fact I think B is a little easier for me because it's pure R - I don't even need to install a database. 

The main benefit I see with B, is that with the database, that first query can take a while, say 3 seconds, whereas calling the .rds is realtime.

I'm going to test both, and take the quickest I suppose.  

I thought maybe there was something fundamental I was overlooking.  Been thinking this a while - as time goes on (Ie. bigger computers), I keep finding myself abandoning databases in the interest of coding pure R to reach realtime.  And it definitely goes against the grain with peers, not to use a database, in favor of a customized (distributed) file system.
